title: Lab 5: Count Regression
text:
Why not a linear model?





DHARMa residual diagnostics for the Gaussian model.




The Gaussian model showed substantial lack of fit. The DHARMa QQ plot strayed far from the diagonal, and the uniformity and outlier tests were significant. The residual-versus-predicted plot also showed systematic quantile deviations, indicating that the residual distribution varied across fitted values. Even though the dispersion test was not significant, this did not resolve the other diagnostic problems. A Gaussian model also assigns probability to negative and non-integer outcomes, whereas physician visits are non-negative counts, and its constant conditional variance assumption may be unsuitable for this outcome. These findings motivate evaluating count-regression models.

title: Lab 5: Count Regression
text:
Interpret the Poisson diagnostics
The full Poisson model showed significant overdispersion (DHARMa dispersion ratio = 7.25, p < .001). The observed number of zeros was 14.91 times the number expected under the fitted model (p < .001). These results indicate that the Poisson model does not adequately capture the variability and zeros in the outcome. Overdispersion can lead to underestimated standard errors, overly narrow confidence intervals, and overly small p-values. However, excess zeros relative to the Poisson model do not necessarily imply a separate zero-generating process. A negative binomial model will therefore be evaluated before considering a zero-inflated or hurdle model.

The NB2 model fit significantly better than the full Poisson model, χ²(1) = 1.212908^{4}, p < .001. The comparison has one degree of freedom because NB2 estimates an additional dispersion parameter. The NB2 dispersion test was not significant (ratio = 1.05, p = 0.392), indicating that the previously detected overdispersion was no longer clear on this diagnostic. So, the Poisson model’s restrictive variance assumption was not supported, and its conventional standard errors and significance tests should not be relied on for inference.
However, the NB2 model continued to under predict zeros (observed/expected ratio = 1.1, p = 0.004). Although this mismatch was much smaller than under Poisson, the observed number of zeros remained approximately 10.44% greater than expected. So, Zero-inflated and hurdle negative binomial models will be evaluated.

title: Lab 5: Count Regression
section: Justify my choice for which model was carried forward
text:
Justify my choice for which model was carried forward
The hurdle negative binomial model was carried forward because it had the lowest AIC and BIC of the candidate models and reproduced the overall number of zeros well (observed/expected ratio = 0.998, p = 0.984). In contrast, ordinary NB2 continued to under predict zeros. The ZINB model also addressed the overall zero-count mismatch, but had higher AIC and BIC than the hurdle model.
The selected model nevertheless retained significant residual overdispersion (ratio = 1.148, p = 0.008) and its residuals differed significantly from the expected uniform distribution. The quantile diagnostic also issued a fitting warning, so its p-value was not relied upon. So, the hurdle model was the best-supported of the candidates considered, rather than a fully adequate description of the data. Later findings are interpreted with this limitation in mind.

Comparing emmeans results with the prediction plot
The emmeans analyses averaged over health and gender, whereas the ggeffects plot held non-focal categorical predictors at their reference levels. For comparisons on the same count-component log scale, these additive control-variable contributions cancel from the insurance contrast because they do not interact with insurance. However, the plotted predictions also combined the zero and count components, while the simple-effects analysis used only the count component. So, differences between the plot and these results reflect both the treatment of control variables and the model quantity being estimated. The count-component log contrasts should not be interpreted as contrasts in overall expected visits.

title: Lab 5: Count Regression
text:
6.7 Interpret the interaction
There was insufficient evidence that the count-component association between chronic conditions and physician visits differed by private insurance status. Adding the interaction did not significantly improve fit, χ²(1) = 0.341, p = 0.559. The chronic-condition slopes were positive in both insurance groups, but their difference was not statistically significant.
Simple-effects comparisons indicated that respondents without private insurance had a lower count-component log parameter than those with insurance at low chronic conditions (log contrast = -0.158, p = 0.014), average chronic conditions (log contrast = -0.136, p = 0.002), and high chronic conditions (log contrast = -0.114, p = 0.028). These tests were not adjusted across the three probing values. The estimated log-scale difference was largest at the low probing value and smallest at the high value, but the non-significant interaction does not support a reliable change in the group difference as chronic conditions increase.
Overall, the results suggest an insurance-group difference in the count component instead of clear evidence of moderation. The original prediction of a stronger chronic-condition slope among respondents with private insurance was not supported. Still, interpretation remains cautious because the selected model retained residual-fit limitations.

title: Lab 5: Count Regression
text:
7.1 Results
Physician visits had a mean of 5.77 and a variance of 45.69, with 15.50% of respondents reporting no visits. The full Poisson model showed pronounced overdispersion (dispersion ratio = 7.246, p < .001) and under predicted the number of zeros (observed-to-simulated zero ratio = 14.906, p < .001). The negative-binomial model fit significantly better than the Poisson model, χ²(1) = 12129.08, p < .001. The NB2 dispersion test was no longer significant (dispersion ratio = 1.046, p = .392), but the model still under predicted zeros (observed-to-simulated zero ratio = 1.104, p = .004), supporting consideration of a separate zero component. Among the NB2, zero-inflated negative-binomial, and hurdle negative-binomial candidates, the hurdle model had the lowest BIC (24426.27), compared with 24436.63 for the zero-inflated model and 24521.03 for NB2, and was carried forward. Still, its residual diagnostics indicated remaining overdispersion (dispersion ratio = 1.148, p = .008) and residuals that differed significantly from the expected uniform distribution (D = 0.029, p < .001). So, The hurdle model was the best-supported candidate among those considered, instead of it being a fully adequate model.
In the selected additive hurdle negative-binomial model, greater numbers of chronic conditions (b = 0.148, 95% CI [0.123, 0.172], p < .001), poor health relative to the reference health category (b = 0.383, 95% CI [0.287, 0.478], p < .001), more years of schooling (b = 0.021, 95% CI [0.012, 0.030], p < .001), and private insurance (b = 0.130, 95% CI [0.045, 0.216], p = .003) were associated with higher log-scale count-component parameters, while adjusting for the other predictors. Excellent health was associated with a lower count-component parameter (b = -0.368, 95% CI [-0.501, -0.236], p < .001), whereas the female–male difference was not statistically significant (b = 0.056, 95% CI [-0.008, 0.121], p = .088). In the zero component, more chronic conditions (b = -0.558, 95% CI [-0.647, -0.470], p < .001), female gender (b = -0.401, 95% CI [-0.573, -0.230], p < .001), more schooling (b = -0.058, 95% CI [-0.082, -0.035], p < .001), and private insurance (b = -0.747, 95% CI [-0.944, -0.550], p < .001) were associated with lower odds of reporting zero physician visits. Excellent health was associated with higher odds of zero visits (b = 0.309, 95% CI [0.029, 0.588], p = .030), whereas poor health was not significantly associated with the odds of zero visits (b = -0.050, 95% CI [-0.363, 0.263], p = .754). Count-component coefficients describe the log-scale parameter of the truncated negative-binomial distribution, instead of effects on overall expected physician visits.
Adding the chronic conditions × private insurance interaction to the count component did not significantly improve model fit, χ²(1) = 0.341, p = .559. The count-component log-scale slope for chronic conditions was positive for respondents without private insurance (b = 0.160, 95% CI [0.111, 0.208], p < .001) and for those with private insurance (b = 0.143, 95% CI [0.115, 0.172], p < .001). Pointwise comparisons indicated lower count-component log parameters for “without private insurance” than respondents with private insurance at low chronic conditions (no − yes log contrast = -0.158, p = .014), average chronic conditions (log contrast = -0.136, p = .002), and high chronic conditions (log contrast = -0.114, p = .028). These comparisons were not adjusted across the three probing values. The estimated log-scale insurance difference was largest at the low probing value and smallest at the high probing value, but remained statistically significant at all three values. However, the non-significant interaction did not support a reliable difference between the chronic-condition slopes. The prediction of a stronger positive association among insured respondents was therefore not supported. So, the additive hurdle model was retained.

title: Lab 5: Count Regression
text:
7.2 Discussion
The findings suggest that chronic conditions and self-perceived health were important correlates of physician visits. More chronic conditions were associated with a higher count-component parameter and lower odds of reporting no visits, suggesting associations with both whether respondents visited a physician and the positive-count process. Compared with average health, poor health was associated with a higher count-component parameter, whereas excellent health was associated with a lower count-component parameter and higher odds of reporting no visits. Together, these patterns are consistent with greater healthcare use among respondents with greater health needs. However, coefficient magnitudes should not be used alone to rank the importance of predictors because the predictors have different measurement scales.
Private insurance and education were also associated with both components of physician use. Respondents with private insurance and those with more schooling had higher count-component parameters and lower odds of zero visits, holding the other predictors constant. Women had lower odds of zero visits than men, but the count-component gender difference was not statistically significant. There was insufficient evidence that private insurance moderated the association between chronic conditions and the count component. Although insurance-group differences were detected at each selected chronic-condition value, those differences did not establish that the chronic-condition slopes differed between groups.
Many limitations should be considered when interpreting these findings. The analysis was observational, so the associations do not establish causal effects. The selected model adjusted only for the included predictors. Other factors, such as income and access to care, could contribute to the observed associations. The data concern older adults surveyed in the United States in the late 1980s, which limits generalization to younger populations and contemporary healthcare settings. Most importantly, although the hurdle negative-binomial model was the best-supported candidate among those considered, its residual diagnostics still indicated overdispersion and residuals that differed significantly from the expected uniform distribution. So, we should interpret its standard errors, confidence intervals, and p-values cautiously. The simple-effects tests were also pointwise comparisons without adjustment across the three probing values. Finally, count-component coefficients describe the truncated distribution’s log-scale parameter, not overall expected visits, which depend on both hurdle components.
